rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause “and you forget yourselves” may be circumstantial to “you command,” making the rebuke concern commanding while self-neglecting, or coordinated and itself the main object of blame.
rows.anchor: جملة : { وتنسون أنفسكم } يجوز أن تكون حالا من ضمير { تأمرون } أو يكون محل التوبيخ

rows.speaker: الفخر
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur rejects the inference attributed to al-Fakhr that a sinner may not enjoin good or forbid wrong: the verse censures a shameful state, not a prohibited act.
rows.anchor: كما نقل عنهم الفخر في ( التفسير ) فإنه ليس المقصود نهي ولا تحريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafs can denote the whole human self, body and spirit; Arabic also uses it for a person’s whole being, as in self-reference and the cited verses.
rows.anchor: والأنفس جمع نفس بسكون الفاء وهي مجموع ذات الإنسان من الهيكل والروح كما هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafs can also mean a part or the inward consciousness: the commentator cites ordinary speech and Qur’anic examples for these uses.
rows.anchor: وتارة على البعض كقول القائل أنكرت نفسي وقوله : { وتنسون أنفسكم } وعلى الإحساس الباطني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafs can denote the spirit responsible for perception; Ibn Ashur promises further explanation when discussing the verse about every soul on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: وتطلق على الروح الذي به الإدراك { إن النفس لأمارة بالسوء } ( يوسف : 53 )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reciting the Torah makes self-neglect especially outrageous: both urging others to righteousness and reading its commands and prohibitions should remind the speaker to reform himself.
rows.anchor: لأن نسيان أنفسهم يكون أغرب وأفظع إذا كان معهم أمران يقلعانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question is an emphatic denial and rebuke, treating them as though reason had disappeared because they neglect themselves despite two reminders of their need to reform.
rows.anchor: استفهاما مستعملا في الإنكار والتوبيخ نزلوا منزلة من انتفى تعقله فأنكر عليهم ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “reason” is treated as intransitive or is inherently intransitive here, underscoring their extreme heedlessness and disordered condition.
rows.anchor: وفعل { تعقلون } منزل منزلة اللازم أو هو لازم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is attached to the preceding statement about Jews and Christians and digresses to expose the polytheists’ analogous misconduct toward Islam.
rows.anchor: عطف على { وقالت اليهود ليست النصارى على شيء } ( البقرة : 113 ) باعتبار ما سبق ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: According to Ibn Abbas, in a report from Ata, the verse was revealed about Arab polytheists; their exclusion of the Prophet and Muslims from Mecca fits the warning that they would enter the mosques only afraid.
rows.anchor: والآية نازلة في مشركي العرب كما في رواية عطاء عن ابن عباس

words: أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ مَا كَانَ لَهُمْ أَن يَدْخُلُوهَآ إِلَّا خَآئِفِينَ
rows.speaker: سعد بن معاذ
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur cites the report of Saad ibn Muadh: Abu Jahl challenged him for circumambulating safely after sheltering the converts, and exclusion recurred at Hudaybiyya.
rows.anchor: كما جاء في حديث سعد بن معاذ حين دخل مكة خفية وقال له أبو جهل

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An alternative account says the verse concerns Nebuchadnezzar’s three campaigns, which culminated in the plunder and destruction of the Jerusalem sanctuary and city and the exile of Israel.
rows.anchor: وقيل نزلت في بختنصر ملك أشور وغزوه بيت المقدس ثلاث غزوات

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another account assigns the verse to the Roman Titus’s conquest of Jerusalem, destruction of the sanctuary, and burning of the Torah; Ibn Ashur says this and the Nebuchadnezzar account do not fit the context.
rows.anchor: وقيل : نزلت في غزو طيطس الروماني لأورشليم سنة 79 قبل المسيح فخرب بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur prefers Ibn Abbas’s account: it fits the warning about fearful entry and the context, where polytheists, like the People of the Book, obstructed Islamic guidance and barred access to the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: والوجه هو التعويل على الرواية الأولى وهي المأثورة عن ابن عباس فالمناسبة أنه بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative min is condemnatory; because it is an indefinite noun in a negative rhetorical question, the meaning is “no one is more unjust.”
rows.anchor: والاستفهام بمن إنكاري ولما كان أصل من أنها نكرة موصوفة أشربت معنى الاستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zulm means violating another’s right by an unwelcome use of it, and also putting something where it does not belong; either sense applies here.
rows.anchor: والظلم الاعتداء على حق الغير بالتصرف فيه بما لا يرضى به ويطلق على وضع الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are exceptionally unjust because they wronged Muslims, who had the strongest claim to the Sacred Mosque, and brought disgrace on themselves among other peoples.
rows.anchor: فقد ظلموا المسلمين من المسجد الحرام وهم أحق الناس به وظلموا أنفسهم بسوء السمعة بين الأمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural “mosques” may magnify the offense; Ibn Ashur compares its use for Noah’s people, who denied the messengers in the plural.
rows.anchor: إما للتعظيم فإن الجمع يجيء للتعظيم كقوله تعالى : { وقوم نوح لما كذبوا الرسل أغرقناهم }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural may encompass the Kaaba and adjoining sacred worship places, including the sanctuary, Maqam Ibrahim, Hatim, Khayf, Mina, and al-Mashar al-Haram.
rows.anchor: وإما لما فيه من أماكن العبادة وهي البيت والمسجد الحرام ومقام إبراهيم والحطيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the general plural warns every person who ruins a mosque or obstructs worship by preventing its rites; the polytheists are foremost among those included.
rows.anchor: وإما لقصد دخول جميع مساجد الله لأنه جمع تعرف بالإضافة ووقع في سياق منع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural pronoun in “enter them” may favor particular, identifiable mosques, since this worldly punishment does not necessarily apply to every person who obstructs a mosque.
rows.anchor: ولعل ضمير الجمع المنصوب في قوله : { أن يدخلوها } يؤيد أن المراد من المساجد مساجد معلومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibited obstruction is depriving qualified worshippers of appointed rites such as circumambulation and congregational prayer.
rows.anchor: والمراد من المنع منع العبادة في أوقاتها الخاصة بها كالطواف والجماعة إذا قصد بالمنع حرمان فريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary closure outside prayer times, preserving a mosque, excluding those unqualified to enter, and barring the polytheist, non-Muslim, sexually impure, or menstruating are not the offense meant here.
rows.anchor: وليس منه غلق المساجد في غير أوقات الجماعة لأن صلاة الفذ لا تفضل في المسجد على غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sa‘y originally means walking and conventionally came to mean purposeful causation; “striving in” takes fi to indicate the purpose, as in “he turned away striving.”
rows.anchor: والسعي أصله المشي ثم صار مجازا مشهورا في التسبب المقصود كالحقيقة العرفية نحو { ثم أدبر يسعى }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the preferred occasion account, blocking worship is literal and ruin is metaphorical causation; on the other accounts, the rulers caused destruction literally while “preventing” worship is metaphorical.
rows.anchor: فالمنع هنا حقيقة على الرواية الأولى المتقدمة في سبب النزول والسعي مجاز في التسبب غير المقصود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence about their entry stands independently to answer the natural question of what punishment follows such injustice, or it may interrupt the clause before the worldly humiliation.
rows.anchor: جملة مستأنفة تغني عن سؤال ناشىء عن قوله : { من أظلم } أو عن قوله : { سعى }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative gathers the three descriptions into a striking portrait; the passage first displays their extraordinary conduct, then states fitting worldly and afterlife punishments.
rows.anchor: والإشارة بأولئك بعد إجراء الأوصاف الثلاثة عليهم للتنبيه على أنهم استحضروا بتلك الأوصاف

words: مَا كَانَ لَهُمْ أَن يَدْخُلُوهَآ إِلَّا خَآئِفِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “It was not for them to enter except fearfully” denies future entry except in fear; كان is past in form, but this construction with أن and the imperfect does not imply past occurrence.
rows.anchor: فإن ما كان إذا وقع أن والمضارع في خبرها تدل على نفي المستقبل وإن كان لفظ ( كان ) لفظ الماضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām indicates entitlement: the threat is that God would end their control of the sanctuary and its rites and give them to Muslims; at the conquest, polytheists entered frightened until the Prophet’s herald proclaimed safety.
rows.anchor: وهذا وعيد بأنهم قدر الله عليهم أن ترفع أيديهم من التصرف في المسجد الحرام وشعائر الله هناك

rows.speaker: كثير من المفسرين
rows.claim: Many commentators take all mosques generally and read fear as humble reverence for God, with the lām expressing restriction; Ibn Ashur rejects this because the demonstrative makes the entry condition a consequence of their prior offense.
rows.anchor: وهذا الوجه وإن فرضه كثير من المفسرين إلا أن مكان اسم الإشارة المؤذن بأن ما بعده ترتب عما قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly humiliation is a second independent sentence, given emphasis by not coordinating it; khizyi means abasement, including the Quraysh leaders’ deaths and captivity at Badr and flight at the conquest.
rows.anchor: وقوله : { لهم في الدنيا خزي } استئناف ثان ولم يعطف على ما قبله ليكون مقصودا الاستئناف اهتماما به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afterlife punishment is coordinated with the worldly one to complete the statement that they face two punishments, one in each realm.
rows.anchor: عطفت على ما قبلها لأنها تتميم لها إذ المقصود من مجموعهما أن لهم عذابين عذابا في الدنيا وعذابا في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation also rebuts polytheists over the Prophet’s post-Hijra change from facing the Kaaba: their exclusion of Muslims from the Sacred Mosque was graver than facing another direction in prayer.
rows.anchor: نزول هذه الآية مؤذن بالاحتجاج على المشركين من سبب انصراف النبيء عن استقبال الكعبة بعد هجرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The placement initially seems puzzling: this verse predicts a future criticism, which one would expect after the change of prayer direction and its abrogating verses.
rows.anchor: قد خفي موقع هذه الآية من الآي التي بعدها لأن الظاهر منها أنها إخبار عن أمر يقع في المستقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent referent of the changed qibla is the former direction, Jerusalem or the east, which was the Jews’ qibla; earlier exegetes did not adequately resolve the placement or context.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد بالقبلة المحولة القبلة المنسوخة وهي استقبال بيت المقدس أعني الشرق وهي قبلة اليهود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur’s preferred context is that earlier praise of Abraham, his religion, and the Kaaba prompts the polytheists to ask why Muhammad turned from the Kaaba to Jerusalem despite claiming Abraham’s religion.
rows.anchor: والذي استقر عليه فهمي أن مناسبة وقوع هذه الآية هنا مناسبة بديعة وهي أن الآيات التي قبلها تكرر فيها التنويه بإبراهيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God places the anticipated taunt before the command to face the Kaaba so the polytheists cannot claim their criticism caused the change; prior allusions to God’s east and west and Jewish and Christian rejection feed the context.
rows.anchor: لئلا يكون القرآن الذي فيه الأمر باستقبال الكعبة نازلا بعد مقالة المشركين فيشمخوا بأنوفهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibrahim apparently faced the Kaaba in prayer and supplication when he built it, intending prayer around it because its interior could not hold the crowds.
rows.anchor: فالظاهر أن إبراهيم عليه السلام لما بنى الكعبة استقبلها عند الدعاء وعند الصلاة وأنه بناها للصلاة حولها

rows.speaker: زيد بن عمرو بن نفيل
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur cites Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl’s poem as evidence that Arabs knew prayer facing the Kaaba; he says there is no evidence Ibrahim faced it from distant locations.
rows.anchor: ويدل عليه قول زيد بن عمرو بن نفيل : عذت بما عاذ به إبراهم مستقبل المعبة وهو قائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The obligation to orient prayer toward the Kaaba from far away appears to be a distinctive feature of this law and one way it completes the religion.
rows.anchor: فيكون الأمر بالتزام الاستقبال في الصلاة من خصائص هذه الشريعة ومن جملة معاني إكمال الدين بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse implies Muslims changed from one prayer direction to another; because the destination was the Kaaba, the prior direction was Jerusalem, as the reports confirm.
rows.anchor: وقد دلت هذه الآية على أن المسلمين كانوا يستقبلون جهة ثم تحولوا عنها إلى جهة أخرى وليست التي تحول إليها المسلمون

words: قَدْ نَرَىٰ تَقَلُّبَ وَجْهِكَ فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ
rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar reports that people at Quba were told during Fajr that revelation had commanded the Kaaba and turned from facing Syria; Ibn Ashur calls this the soundest report and the decisive account, transmitted by the Muwatta, Bukhari, and Muslim routes.
rows.anchor: عن ابن دينار عن ابن عمر ( بينما الناس في صلاة الصبح بقباء

words: قَدْ نَرَىٰ تَقَلُّبَ وَجْهِكَ فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ
rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: In Muslim’s report from Anas, a man told Banu Salima, already one rakah into Fajr, that the qibla had changed, and they turned while bowing.
rows.anchor: ثانيها : حديث مسلم عن أنس بن مالك وفيه ( فمر رجل من بني سلمة

words: قَدْ نَرَىٰ تَقَلُّبَ وَجْهِكَ فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ
rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Bara reports in Bukhari and Muslim that after sixteen or seventeen months facing Jerusalem, the Prophet turned to the Kaaba; an Ansar congregation changed to it after a worshipper informed them during Asr.
rows.anchor: عن البراء بن عازب قال كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم صلى نحو بيت المقدس ستة عشر شهرا أو سبعة عشر شهرا

words: قَدْ نَرَىٰ تَقَلُّبَ وَجْهِكَ فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur reconciles Fajr and Asr in the reports by assigning them to different localities; he says other conflicting reports cited by al-Qurtubi have unsound chains.
rows.anchor: وحمل ذكر صلاة الصبح في روايتي ابن عمر وأنس بن مالك وذكر صلاة العصر في رواية البراء كل على أهل مكان مخصوص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qibla was changed in Rajab of 2 AH, two months before Badr; another report dates it to Tuesday, mid-Sha‘ban of that year.
rows.anchor: فتحويل القبلة كان في رجب سنة اثنتين من الهجرة قبل بدر بشهرين وقيل يوم الثلاثاء نصف شعبان منها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority say the Prophet faced the Kaaba in Mecca when prayer was prescribed, then turned toward Jerusalem after reaching Medina to accommodate the Jews; Ibn Ashur calls that stated motive weak.
rows.anchor: فالجمهور على أنه لما فرضت عليه الصلاة بمكة كان يستقبل الكعبة فلما قدم المدينة استقبل بيت المقدس تألفا لليهود قاله بعضهم وهو ضعيف

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A further view says he faced Jerusalem from a place where the Kaaba lay eastward, so he faced both; Ibn Ashur says this view is unsound.
rows.anchor: وقيل كان يستقبل بيت المقدس وهو في مكان يجعل الكعبة أمامه من جهة الشرق فيكون مستقبلا الكعبة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and the majority say God commanded the Prophet by revelation to face Jerusalem and later abrogated it for the Kaaba, citing the verse about the former qibla.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس والجمهور أوجبه الله عليه بوحي ثم نسخه باستقبال الكعبة ودليلهم قوله تعالى : { وما جعلنا القبلة التي كنت عليها }

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says the Prophet could choose either the Kaaba or Jerusalem and chose Jerusalem to accommodate the Jews.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري كان مخيرا بين الكعبة وبيت المقدس واختار بيت المقدس استئلافا لليهود

rows.speaker: الحسن وعكرمة وأبو العالية
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, Ikrima, and Abu al-Aliya attribute the Jerusalem direction to the Prophet’s own judgment: he followed the prior two religions’ qibla while wishing for a command to face the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وعكرمة وأبو العالية : كان ذلك عن اجتهاد من النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وعلى هذا القول

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: The “fools” who criticized the change are variously identified as Jews, hypocrites, or Quraysh disbelievers; al-Zajjaj cites the latter taunt that Muhammad missed his homeland and would soon return to their religion, attributed to al-Bara, Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan.
rows.anchor: وقيل كفار قريش قالوا اشتاق محمد إلى بلده وعن قريب يرجع إلى دينكم ذكره الزجاج

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi reports that Abu Said ibn al-Mualla was the first Muslim to pray toward the Kaaba, but Ibn Ashur says the report is weak.
rows.anchor: وروى القرطبي أن أول من صلى نحو الكعبة من المسلمين أبو سعيد بن المعلى وفي الحديث ضعف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fā in “then We will turn you” marks sequence and stresses the explicit promise after the preliminary, implicit reassurance that God sees the Prophet’s gaze.
rows.anchor: والفاء في { فلنولينك } فاء التعقيب لتأكيد الوعد بالصراحة بعد التمهيد لها بالكناية في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawliya here means directing the Prophet toward a qibla; qibla is expressed as an expanded second object, originally “turn you from a qibla.”
rows.anchor: فمعنى { فلنولينك قبلة } لنوجهنك إلى قبلة ترضاها . فانتصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to face the Kaaba follows the promise immediately; its two emphases and sequencing express exceptional kindness and attention to the Prophet’s wish.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أن تولية وجهه للكعبة سيحصل عقب هذا الوعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s inclination toward the Kaaba seeks a good: it is the house most suited to signify monotheism and its qibla marks Islam’s independence from the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: وعبر بترضاها للدلالة على أن ميله إلى الكعبة ميل لقصد الخير بناء على أن الكعبة أجدر بيوت الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “pleased” suggests affection grounded in reflection, befitting the Prophet’s reasoned preference for a lasting benefit after the temporary reason for facing Jerusalem ended; the verse warns against following others’ desires.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الرضى مشعرا بالمحبة الناشئة عن تعقل اختير في هذا المقام دون تحبها أو تهواها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command follows the promise and hastens its fulfillment; prayer is understood from the context of the dispute with the fools, and the next clause extends the command to the whole community.
rows.anchor: وقوله : { فول وجهك } تفريع على الوعد وتعجيل به والمعنى فول وجهك في حالة الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shatr with fatḥa on shīn and sukūn on ṭā means direction or side; Qatada glosses it as “toward.”
rows.anchor: والشطر بفتح الشين وسكون الطاء الجهة والناحية وفسره قتادة بتلقاء

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Kab’s reading has تلقاء (“toward”) in place of shatr, supporting the directional sense.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قرأه أبي بن كعب

rows.speaker: الجبائي وعبد الجبار
rows.claim: Al-Jubba’i and Abd al-Jabbar interpret shatr as the middle of the sanctuary, figuratively identifying the Kaaba; Abd al-Jabbar argues prayer aimed elsewhere in the mosque is invalid and this reading gives shatr a function.
rows.anchor: وفسر الجبائي وعبد الجبار الشطر هنا بأنه وسط الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prior promise highlights how much the Prophet’s wish is valued, especially through the description “a qibla you are pleased with.”
rows.anchor: فائدته إظهار الاهتمام برغبة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وأنها بحيث يعتنى بها كما دل عليه وصف القبلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuwallika means “we direct you”; the verb’s sense is linked to walī as attachment or connection when physical nearness is not intended.
rows.anchor: ومعنى ( نولينك ) نوجهنك ، وفي التوجيه قرب معنوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walla may take the face and destination as two objects, with a third introduced by ʿan to mark turning away; it can also be treated as intransitive with the other objects understood.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن تعديته إلى مفعول ثان من قبيل الحذف والتقدير ولى وجهه إلى كذا ثم يعدونه إلى مفعول ثالث بحرف عن
